latest_release.name: v2026.11.12: `mise audit` and `mise upgrade --vulnerable` for known vulnerabilities
latest_release.body:
New `mise audit` and `mise upgrade --vulnerable` commands check your tools against OSV.dev advisories and upgrade the affected ones. This release also adds `mise prune --system`, a per-tool `bump = false` option, and more flexible dotfile groups. It fixes lockfile handling for platforms a tool has no build for, PATH setup for locked task tools, and Temurin hotfix versions from `.sdkmanrc`.

## Added

### Vulnerability auditing

- **`mise audit`** checks each tool version your config uses against the [OSV.dev](https://osv.dev) database and lists the advisories that affect it. It exits 1 when it finds any, so you can use it to gate CI. `mise audit node python` checks only the tools you name, and `--json` prints `{"vulnerabilities": [...], "unchecked": [...]}`. [#15942](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15942) (@jdx, @johnstegeman)

  ```console
  $ mise audit
  Tool        Version  ID                   Severity  Fixed    Summary
  npm:lodash  4.17.15  GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm  high      4.17.21  Command Injection in lodash
  ...
  mise not checked, no known advisory source: zig@0.13.0
  ```

  - These tools are covered:
    - registry packages (`npm:`, `pipx:`, `cargo:`, `gem:`, `go:`, `dotnet:`)
    - tools released from GitHub or GitLab (`github:`, `aqua:`, `packslip:`, `gitlab:`), matched by repository and release tag
    - the core tools go (as the Go standard library), node, python, deno, bun and erlang
  - Anything else, including tools from private registries or self-hosted `api_url`s, is listed as **not checked** and is never reported as clean.
  - The audit fails if a configured version doesn't resolve. It needs network access to `api.osv.dev`, so it fails in offline mode. Only tool names and versions are sent.
- **`mise upgrade --vulnerable`** limits `mise upgrade` to installed tools with a known vulnerability. Upgrades stay within the configured range unless you add `--bump`. `--dry-run`, `--exclude` and `--inactive` work as usual. mise warns when an affected tool has no fix in range, when the target version is still affected, and when a tool could not be checked. [#15942](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15942) (@jdx, @johnstegeman)

### Upgrades and pruning

- **Per-tool `bump` option.** `bump = false` keeps a tool out of `mise upgrade --bump` and `mise outdated --bump`. Those commands still upgrade it within its version request but don't rewrite its entry in `mise.toml`. This helps when tools like topgrade run `mise upgrade` for you and can't pass `-x`. If you name the tool (`mise upgrade node --bump`), it is still bumped. This option isn't available in `.tool-versions`. [#15947](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15947) (@jdx, @gitfool)

  ```toml
  [tools]
  node = { version = "lts", bump = false }
  ```

- **`mise prune --system`** removes unused versions from the system installs directory, using `sudo` when that directory is owned by root. A version is kept if a config file your user has loaded (including `/etc/mise/config.toml`) still selects it, or if a running process you can inspect uses it. mise can't see other users' configs, so it warns about that. Plain `mise prune` still leaves system installs alone. [#15949](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/15949) (@jdx, @ioweb-gr)

  ```sh
  mise prune --system --dry-run
  mise prune --system
  ```

  `mise upgrade` now also cleans up system installs it replaces, after the `upgrade.prune_after` grace period. Before, old versions piled up indefinitely. This background cleanup never asks for a sudo password. If removing a version would need `sudo`, mise keeps it and tells you to run `mise prune --system` or upgrade with `--prune`. `mise uninstall` of a system version in a root-owned directory now uses `sudo` instead of failing. `mise reshim --system` no longer drops the shim for a system version that you also have in your own installs directory.

## What is mise? mise (pronounced "meez", short for _mise-en-place_) manages a project's dev tools, environment variables, and tasks from one `mise.toml` that works across your shell, editor, and CI: ```toml [tools] node = "24" python = "3.14" rust = "stable" "cargo:cargo-nextest" = "0.9" "github:BurntSushi/ripgrep" = "15" "npm:prettier" = "3" [env] NODE_ENV = "development" _.file = ".env" _.path = "./node_modules/.bin" [tasks.build] description = "Build the application" run = "npm run build" [tasks.test] description = "Run the test suite" depends = ["build"] run = "pytest && npm test" ``` - Install [dev tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/) such as Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, and Terraform from a [registry of 1,000+ tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/registry.html) or directly from [backends](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/backends/) like GitHub releases, Aqua, Cargo, npm, and PyPI, with separate versions per project. - Load [environment variables](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/), `.env` files, `PATH` entries, virtualenvs, and [secrets](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/secrets/) automatically as you enter a directory. - Run [tasks](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/) defined in `mise.toml` or as scripts in `mise-tasks/`, with dependencies, parallel execution, file watching, and the project's tools and environment already configured. - Set up a machine with [`mise bootstrap`](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html) and [`mise dot apply`](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) to apply system packages, dotfiles, Git repositories, macOS defaults, and background services. Each part works without the others, so you can start with a single tool or task. A project that already has `.nvmrc`, `.python-version`, or another [idiomatic version file](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/versions.html#idiomatic-version-files) can keep it: mise reads those files once you enable them. [![Demo of mise managing tools](./docs/tapes/demo.gif)](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html) See the [demo transcript](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html#transcript) for the commands shown above. ## Quickstart ### 1. Install mise On macOS or Linux: ```sh curl -fsSL https://mise.run | sh ~/.local/bin/mise --version ``` On Windows, run `irm https://mise.run/powershell | iex` in PowerShell, or `winget install jdx.mise`. For Homebrew, apt, dnf, Scoop, and other package managers, see [Installing mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/installing-mise.html). The installer places the binary at `~/.local/bin/mise`. If `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH` yet, run `~/.local/bin/mise` in place of `mise` until you activate mise in step 4. ### 2. Run a tool without changing your shell ```sh mise exec node@24 -- node --version # v24.x.x ``` [`mise exec`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/exec.html) downloads Node.js 24 if needed and runs the command after `--` with that version on `PATH`. Your shell and config files stay untouched. ### 3. Configure a project Create a project directory, select Node.js 24, set an environment variable, and add a task: ```sh mkdir my-project && cd my-project mise use node@24 mise set NODE_ENV=development mise tasks add hello -- node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)" ``` These commands install Node.js 24 and write `mise.toml`: ```toml [tools] node = "24" [env] NODE_ENV = "development" [tasks.hello] run = "node -e 'console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)'" ``` Run the task with [`mise run`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/run.html): ```sh mise run hello # [hello] $ node -e 'console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)' # v24.x.x development ``` Commit `mise.toml` so teammates and CI get the same setup when they run `mise install` or `mise run`. `"24"` requests the latest release in the Node.js 24 series; run `mise lock` to record exact versions and checksums in a [lockfile](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/mise-lock.html), or `mise use --global node@24` to set a personal default in `~/.config/mise/config.toml`. ### 4. Activate mise in your shell (optional) Shell activation updates `PATH` and project environment variables whenever you change directories, so you can invoke `node` directly without `mise exec`. If you installed with `mise.run`, run the command for your shell once, then open a new terminal: ```sh # bash echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc # zsh echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate zsh)"' >> "${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zshrc" # fish mkdir -p ~/.config/fish echo '~/.local/bin/mise activate fish | source' >> ~/.config/fish/config.fish ``` If a package manager installed mise, use `mise` in place of `~/.local/bin/mise`. With Homebrew, fish activates mise without this step. For PowerShell, Nushell, Elvish, Xonsh, and IDE or CI shims, see [Shell setup](https://mise.jdx.dev/shell-setup.html) and [Shims](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html). ## Everyday commands | Command | Action | | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | `mise use node@24` | Install a tool and record it in the current project's `mise.toml` | | `mise use --global node@24` | Install a tool and set it as your global default | | `mise install` | Install all tools declared in the active config files | | `mise exec -- ` | Run a command with the project's tools and environment | | `mise run ` | Run a project task with its dependencies, tools, and environment | | `mise set KEY=value` | Set an environment variable in `mise.toml` | | `mise env` | Print the resolved environment variables and `PATH` changes | | `mise ls --current` | List the tool versions active in the current directory | | `mise outdated` | List tools with newer releases than the installed version | | `mise upgrade` | Install those newer releases | | `mise lock` | Write exact tool versions and checksums to `mise.lock` | | `mise config ls` | Show the config files loaded for the current directory | | `mise doctor` | Check your mise installation, shell activation, and configuration | ## Set up a machine with mise bootstrap Beyond project directories, `~/.config/mise/config.toml` can declare the state of your machine: ```toml [bootstrap.packages] "apt:build-essential" = "latest" "brew:jq" = "latest" [bootstrap.repos] "~/src/app" = { url = "https://github.com/you/app.git" } [dotfiles] "~/.zshrc" = { mode = "track" } ``` Preview and apply the configuration, or bootstrap a new machine directly from a Git repository: ```sh mise bootstrap --dry-run mise bootstrap mise bootstrap --adopt you/dotfiles ``` See [Bootstrap](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html) and [Dotfiles](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) for supported package managers, dotfile tracking and templating, services, and remote SSH targets. ## Documentation | Topic | Guides | | ----------------------------- |
